pieces.title: 3 Phrases That End Any Meeting · “Is this a decision or a discussion?”

linkedin.label: LinkedIn
linkedin.caption:
"Is this a decision or a discussion?"

Two completely different meetings. Different prep, different pace, different exit. And almost nobody says which one they booked.

The invite said "sync". It was a decision. Half the room came ready to chat, the other half came ready to vote. Both left annoyed, for opposite reasons.

Half of all bad meetings are two meetings happening in the same room at the same time. Ask the question in the first minute and you get one meeting back.

Decision or discussion: which one do you get more of? 👇

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"Is this a decision or a discussion?" Ask it first. Save everyone an hour.

Two different meetings, same invite. One half shows up to decide, the other half shows up to talk it through. Nobody says which one they booked. Everybody leaves convinced the others weren't listening.

Half of all bad meetings are two meetings happening at once. I flag it so you don't have to.

Swipe → slide 4 is the truth. Slide 5 is me being smug about it.

pieces.title: The Art Of Saying No Without Saying No · “I don’t have bandwidth” is not a real sentence

linkedin.label: LinkedIn
linkedin.caption:
"I don't have bandwidth this sprint."

Usually said in a week that still found room for a sync about the sync.

Saying no is fine. Saying no through the calendar costs more: the real reason never gets discussed, so the same request comes back next sprint and gets the same answer.

"Not now, this matters more" is a real sentence. It starts a conversation.

What's your team's favorite way to say no without saying no?

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"I don't have bandwidth" is the politest no in the building.

It sounds like a capacity problem. It's a priority call nobody wants to make out loud. So the request comes back next sprint, and gets the same polite no.

"Not now, this matters more" takes four more seconds and saves a sprint.

pieces.title: 3 Phrases That End Any Meeting · “Who’s the owner and by when?”

linkedin.label: LinkedIn
linkedin.caption:
"Who's the owner and by when?"

The fastest way to end a meeting. Six people discover a hard stop in real time.

Collaboration is free right up until a name goes next to it. So the meeting ends on "great discussion," and the list leaves the room unowned.

A to-do list with no names is a to-do list for nobody.

How many of your action items have a real owner?

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"Who's the owner and by when?" The question that empties a room.

Ask it and watch the calendars open. Suddenly everyone has a hard stop, a conflict, a "let me check with my team."

Nobody minds agreeing. Everybody minds being named.

pieces.title: The 1-On-1 Survival Kit · “Same time next week?”

linkedin.label: LinkedIn
linkedin.caption:
"Same time next week?"

Thirty careful minutes, and the most sincere moment was booking the next one.

Consistency matters. It just isn't proof that anything moved. The same blocker, raised politely three weeks in a row, is still a blocker. It now has a recurring invite.

If nothing changed since last week, the meeting didn't happen. It recurred.

Do your 1-on-1s move anything, or just repeat?

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"Same time next week?" The one question in a 1-on-1 nobody hesitates on.

Thirty careful minutes. Updates, a few "all good", the one thing nobody raised. Then the calendar question, answered instantly, with real conviction.

Showing up weekly is the floor. The job is what moves between two sessions. Nothing moved? Then it wasn't a 1-on-1. It was a rerun.

Your last 1-on-1: did anything move?

pieces.title: What They Say Vs What They Mean · “Let’s align offline”

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"Let's align offline." Two people will align. Six will find out later.

The decision walks out of the call with two people and walks back in as a fact. Everyone else gets it later, phrased as if they had been there. Nodding along to a decision you never saw is now a core skill.

Offline is fine. Offline with no recap is how trust leaks. Whatever gets parked for offline, I write it down with a name next to it. Nobody hears it thirdhand.

Ever found out a decision secondhand?

tiktok.caption: POV: the decision left the call with two people. You were the other six.

pieces.title: Tweet 19:00 et carte Instagram 22:00 · Nobody is out of time

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.caption:
"I don't have time" is a sentence. "It's not my priority" is the translation.

I sit in a lot of meetings. Nobody runs out of time for what they care about. They run out for everything else.

So I make a meeting earn its slot.
Before: we name the one goal it's for.
During: I flag when the talk drifts off it.
After: what landed, what got dropped, and next steps with a priority and a due date.

The rest can wait. It was going to anyway.

What did you "not have time" for this week? I won't tell your calendar.
